shortQuestions: The title shows that the poem is an extract (lines) from Goldsmith's longer poem 'The Deserted Village'. It describes how a once happy and lively village, Auburn, has been deserted because the rich landlords seized the land and the peasants were forced to leave — the title reflects the poet's sorrow at this loss.

The poet pictures 'sweet Auburn', the loveliest village of the plain, where health and plenty cheered the hard-working peasants; spring came early and summer stayed late; there were humble cottages, cultivated farms, a brook, a busy mill, a church on the hill and a hawthorn bush with seats beneath its shade for lovers and the old.

(a) 'Loitered over thy green' — wandered leisurely over the village common/green fields. (b) 'Talking age' — the old people who sat together chatting. (c) 'Seats of my youth' — the places where the poet spent his happy childhood. (d) 'The village train' — the group/crowd of villagers who gathered for sports and games.
The poem is written in heroic couplets — iambic pentameter lines rhyming in pairs; the rhyme scheme is AABBCC…

The land suffers greatly and falls a prey to quickly spreading evils where wealth gathers in the hands of a few rich people while the ordinary men (peasants) decline and suffer. Goldsmith means that a country is truly ruined when riches increase but the people who are its real strength are reduced to poverty and forced away.

Examples: 'Sweet smiling village, loveliest of the lawn'; 'the busy mill'; 'decent church that topped the neighbouring hill'; 'Ill fares the land, to hastening ills a prey' (repetition of the l / h sounds).
activities: The poet calls the bold peasantry 'their country's pride' because they are the real backbone of a nation: they work hard, produce food, are honest, simple and healthy, and keep the country strong. Princes and lords can be made again by a king's word ("a breath can make them, as a breath has made"), but once a strong peasantry is destroyed, it can never be replaced.

Debate points — For modernisation of villages: electricity, roads, schools, hospitals, mobile networks, better farming methods, more income. Against: loss of simplicity, joint family system and community spirit, migration to cities, pollution, imitation of urban fashions. Speakers get 1–2 minutes each; the conclusion can stress progress while preserving good village values.
